newsitem.title: CANADA: Bank Montreal urges foreign competition.
newsitem.headline: Bank Montreal urges foreign competition.

text.p: Canada's protected banking sector should be thrown open to foreign competitors and Canadian banks allowed to get bigger to compete against global rivals, an influential Canadian banker said on Wednesday.

Canadian laws which restrict mergers among the so-called Big Six banks should be relaxed and ownership rules scrapped or modified, Bank of Montreal chairman Matthew Barrett, said in a speech to Toronto's business community.
"What was once protection for the country has become a prison for our banks. I believe we should throw the doors wide open to traffic in both directions," he said.

In an era of economic globalization, Barrett said the distinction between domestic and international markets is being eroded. North American economies are steadily integrating due partly to free trade agreements.
"I am absolutely confident that sooner rather than later, the new U.S. megabanks and the highly competitive U.S. niche players will look north of the border," he said.

In order to match their competitors in service, sales, productivity and marketing, Canadian banks will have to get bigger. "We don't want to be the local hardware store, waiting helplessly for Wal-Mart or Home Depot to arrive," he said.
Barrett said Canadian banks should be given the freedom to merge, "whenever the logic of the emerging marketplace makes that desirable."
Canadian laws at present discourage bank mergers by limiting individual investors to a 10 percent stake in domestic banks.

"We should think very seriously about removing or modifying the 10 percent ownership rule, which depresses the market value of our banks' shares and puts them at a disadvantage in the international market for mergers and acquisitions," Barrett said.

Canadian accounting rules which make it harder for banks to make acquisitions abroad should also be changed, Barrett said. He is the latest Canadian banker to push for changes to bank rules ahead of the federal government's review of Canada's Bank Act in 1997.

Earlier this year, Royal Bank of Canada chairman John Cleghorn said he is willing to see barriers to foreign banks lifted if it persuaded the federal government to allow the major banks to grow domestically.
Foreign banks are currently not allowed to open Canadian branches with access to their parent firms' capital.
Barrett also took aim at the "dense thicket of myths" that have grown up around the Canadian banking industry and block its attempts to grow.
Recent record profits and the banks' dominance in regular banking, trust and brokerage sectors have attracted a lot of bank bashing by consumers, politicians and competitors.

Earlier this year, the banks lost a bid to expand further into insurance and auto leasing. Governments have also slapped special taxes on the banks. Barrett said Canadian bankers should be more aggressive in defending their industry, which he called a "threatened national institution."
